p-story.s: Ideas came from a free brainstorm in a notebook, in Malayalam and English, around relationships, culture and Kerala's own contradictions. Of the keywords it produced, "cultural separation in Kerala" was chosen because the project was made in Kerala.

groups: A man's tools interacting with each other
No worry about preserving culture and language
Why should I need a culture?

p-story.s: Instead of an obvious argument between two groups, lateral "what if" questions were asked. These were the shortlisted candidates:

items: What if a Malayali businessman finds a Tamil child?
What if a boy is caught between obedience to Malayali parents and love for a North-Indian girl?
What if the maps of various states argue with each other about ideologies?
What if coconuts want to escape from Kerala?
What if birds of each state want to get educated?
What if costumes representing each culture enter a beauty contest?
What if animals of each state argue about religion?
What if languages want a cross-cultural collaboration?

p-story.s2: The winner was "What if coconuts want to escape from Kerala?", because coconuts are the word most tied to Kerala: the name itself means the land of coconut trees.

p-story.s: Following John Truby, a wish list of topics that excite the writer was drawn up: flying, protest, investigation, an adventurous trip and relationships. Each was crossed with the coconut idea to turn it into new what-if questions.

rows: What if an Unidentified Flying Object made of coconuts lands in Kerala?
What if a coconut wants to address his complaints about Keralites to a cloud?
What if coconuts go on strike to stop being used as products in Kerala?
What if a coconut wants to obtain a secret plan that stops humans from exploiting them?
What if all coconuts disappear one day and Keralites start investigating?
What if a murder happens among the coconuts?
What if coconuts want to explore an alien world?
What if all the coconuts are killed one day and only one is left?
What if a coconut falls in love with a Malayali girl?

p-story.s: The world was built before the plot: one night in 22nd-century Kerala, with conflict on three levels, and answers to who the characters are, what the world values and what its rituals are.
Not every idea from the setting could fit, so the situations that work best together were brainstormed. These were the candidates:

items: What if scientists in Kerala develop intelligence in coconuts?
What if coconuts set up a world of their own, hidden and separate from Kerala?
What if coconuts find out that Keralites are trying to track them?
What if commando coconuts are sent to Kerala to destroy the attempt to locate Coconut World?
What if a coconut from Coconut World is captured by Keralites?
What if coconuts and Keralites fight for survival?

p-story.s2: The commando situation won because it holds all three levels of conflict at once: the commando coconut, his Boss and the lady scientist, all in the same space.

p-story.s: "Kera Lady" and "Kera Laila" were shortlisted because both spell Kerala in their first letters. Kera Laila won: Kera means coconut, and Laila is an Arabic name meaning night.

Nine well-known story models were compared side by side, not as steps but as different ways of cutting the same arc from beginning to end. Dramatica and McKee were chosen as the backbone because they build the story's foundation rather than its surface.

Dramatica treats a story as one grand argument, seen through four throughlines at once. Each throughline lives in its own domain and has a concern, a benchmark and a few story elements, so no point of view is left out.
p-story.s2: It then sets the order of each throughline's four types as signposts, one per act, joined by three journeys. That keeps every act moving all four perspectives forward together, which is what makes the argument feel complete.

p-story.s: McKee sees story as values that change under pressure, and advises working backwards from the climax. Every one of the twelve scenes turns a value from positive to negative or back, driven by conflict on three levels.

Three models merged into one 8-stage circle: Hauge’s six stages drive the outer journey, Weiland’s pinch points and moment of truth power the middle, and Campbell’s mythic circle lets the story end where it began, transformed.

p-reel.s: The story was drawn shot by shot with rough characters, translating abstract ideas into clear, unambiguous pictures.

p-reel.ls: The boards were not about drawing well. Characters were sketched from first imagination, with no design detail, so the whole story could be put into pictures as fast as possible. The aim was the most story information in the least time, with each action shown clearly enough that it needs no explaining.

Actions that read clearly, with no ambiguity

p-reel.s: A film works in time, so the boards were filmed with a phone and cut together, faking the intended camera moves, to see how everything fits in time. It also gave the first estimate of the film’s length: about 6 minutes.

The camera tracks Kera as he sneaks along, then swings up to the alert flashing on Laila’s screen.

p-reel.s: Where the storyboard got the story down fast, thumbnailing slowed down to design each key frame. Every key shot was drawn in several variations, and each was judged on how well its shapes, placement and values carried the power, emotion and information of that moment.

p-medium.s: The animatic fixed time and look; the medium had to carry the deeper layers. Digital 3D (CGI) was chosen for its range of possibilities, despite its heavy technical groundwork.

p-char.s: Before any drawing, each lead was interviewed like a real person: role, age, home, work, friends and enemies, faith, outlook and backstory. The answers decide how each one sees right and wrong, and that is what drives the conflict.

items.job: Commando-in-chief, head of the security division
items.view: Optimistic at heart, despite the Boss’s constant hate for humans
items.belief: Agnostic. Lets the Boss decide right and wrong, but senses a morality beyond him
items.back: Built by the Boss as his favourite disciple. When his agents failed to get Laila’s data, he was sent himself.

items.goal: Bring the coconuts back to Kerala
items.view: Optimistic, despite a life of hardship
items.belief: Muslim. God alone defines right and wrong
items.friends: Women in her scientist peer group
items.enemies: None by choice; some colleagues reject her views
items.back: Her father gave coconuts intelligence and was blamed when they fled; he, her mother and her husband died in a riot. Her son left to find a toy coconut and never came back.

items.view: Pessimistic; always expects the worst from humans
items.belief: Atheist. Morality is his to dictate
items.friends: None; only a soft spot for Kera
items.enemies: Humans, who he believes will exploit coconuts
items.back: He was the coconut Laila’s father experimented on. Feeling oppressed, he led every coconut out of Kerala to a hidden world in the sky.

dg.alt: Worldview map: Laila optimistic with objective morality, the Boss pessimistic with dictated morality, Kera optimistic but in between, moving towards Laila
dg.note: Laila and the Boss sit at opposite corners. Kera starts in between: hopeful by nature but taking his morality from the Boss. The dotted arrow is his arc, towards Laila’s side.

p-char.s: The Enneagram is a personality map often used in psychology and business. It also suits fiction, because it says what a character wants, what they fear, and how they change. Each lead got one type.

basics: Everyone carries a mix, but one type leads from birth.
Each has strengths to share and something to learn from the others.
Under pressure a person slides towards one type; at their best they grow into another.

items.want: Safety, and loyalty to his Boss above all
items.fear: Constant worry and doubt; he expects the worst and can’t trust anyone
stress: Anxious about results and his image as the favourite
grow: Calm, open, able to make peace with others
items.wing: Investigator (5): he questions and analyses everything

items.want: Principles, integrity and putting wrongs right
items.fear: Anger at injustice; she takes wrong actions to heart
stress: Feels misunderstood and denies her own needs
grow: Embraces life with joy and hope
items.wing: Helper (2): she leads with compassion and mercy

items.want: Control and power over every world
items.fear: Fury when anyone defies him; blind to his own flaws
stress: Turns paranoid, watching everyone through his spies
grow: Love and compassion: the step he never takes
items.wing: Enthusiast (7): charismatic, a speaker who brainwashes

p-char.s2: In the circle above, each arrow points the way a type grows. Read with the cards: Kera starts unhealthy and grows towards the Peacemaker, which is where his story ends. Laila starts healthy, and the Boss stays average because he never takes his step towards compassion.

p-char.s: Robert McKee says true character shows in the choices a person makes under pressure, so every character is designed to bring out the hero's dimensions. Each lead was given four basic traits; the clashes between them became the conflict, and each was finally reduced to two words.

Every trait from the delineations had to read in silhouette alone, so each one was tied to a basic shape. Each character is built from a primary shape, which sets who they are, and a secondary shape that bends it.

chars.d: Friendly at heart, but unsteady: a round body under a top-heavy wedge.
Stable and kind. The simplest silhouette, like her personality: a circle on a pole, like a tree.
Dangerous and immovable: a sharp wedge on a heavy, boxy base.

flow: Part by part: body, head, processing unit, arms, hands, legs, shoes

finals.d: teardrop body, plate roof, rod arms

p-char.s: The silhouettes were turned into basic 3D forms in a digital sculpting tool.
Facial features were explored by painting over the forms. Laila needed the most variations, since her silhouette was so simple.
Laila is the only human, so the golden ratio was used to re-proportion her face and make it more human.
All characters were sculpted in fine detail. Topology was not yet a concern.
The sculpts were placed side by side to set relative scale, so size itself tells the power dynamics.
Laila's son appears only in photographs, so he was designed lightly, just enough for the backstory frames.

p-env.s: Alappuzha is the obvious coconut location, but the story needed hills, cliffs and fog. Munnar in Idukki fitted better, and its mood could be rebuilt with matte painting.
Karimannoor near Thodupuzha, where the project was made, was photographed as a stand-in for Munnar.
The photos and online references were turned into quick sketches: a visual library for building the environment.

p-model.s: 2D model sheets bridged the drawings and 3D, with a rough costume draped on Laila.
Topology was planned on paper and over expressions, focusing on how each face moves from rest to its deformed shapes.
Each model was rebuilt with clean topology: major face loops first, then continuous edge flow everywhere else.
The terrain was sculpted for height, then detailed with height fields. Its crests and troughs stage the story's dynamics.
An antenna shaped like a coconut tree shows that the real palms are gone. It was modelled procedurally, so variations come for free.
Laila's lab has the coconut-tree antenna at its exact centre, and the building was designed around it.
The lab interior was planned room by room, from plan sketches to the finished model.
Props carry hidden meaning: a photo frame of a child with a coconut explains Laila's motive, and her gun reads as terror from the front but self-protection from behind.

p-rig.s: Each rig follows its character's personality: Laila flexible, the Boss mechanical, and Kera in between.

items: Discrete connection · partly flexible, partly mechanical

p-rig.s: Body parts were ranked into a joint hierarchy so they deform in the right order, not all with equal weight.
Joints were placed and oriented to rotate in natural arcs, then skinned. The body was rigged first for body language, then the face for expression.
Expression combinations were explored per character to find how each part of the face should deform.
Facial controls were grouped into on-screen interfaces, so an animator without technical knowledge can drive each face.
Every rig was tested with extreme poses and expressions, so mistakes surfaced before animation.
Props with their own movement got dedicated rigs.
Simple props, like a door that slides or swings, needed only a single move or rotate control.

r-change.s: The Boss's rig broke when imported for animation. Instead of redoing it, the Boss was removed and given only a voice through Kera's earpiece, which made the smallest object in the film its antagonist.

r-dialog.s: Most of the story is told visually, so dialog was used sparingly to carry subtext, like the Boss's "They and us will never go side by side".
The film is action-driven, so instead of a full screenplay a short dialog script was written in Malayalam and translated.
Two voice artists were recorded separately in a studio, and Laila was deliberately left without dialog.
The best parts of many takes were cut and blended into one continuous voice track.

r-anim.s: Production started with a shot list based on the animatic, so every shot was planned before animating.
Each shot was acted out on camera as reference for locomotion, weight and body language.
From the reference footage, key movements were thumbnailed to plan each shot and apply the principles of animation.
A hybrid approach was used: block the key poses for story first, then refine part by part in layers.
Subtext lives in the face, so dialog was broken into visemes for a two-stage lip sync, then the face was animated in layers.
Shots were framed in two ways: discovered, like a camera operator exploring a set, and developed, like an artist arranging an exact composition.

items: Explore the set through the viewfinder
Change the scene to fit an exact composition

r-anim.s: The previz is the CGI blueprint, giving every department the tone and complexity of each shot.

r-surf.s: Surfacing ran alongside animation on the same topology. Models were cut into UV shells, like sewing a garment in reverse.
The curved shells were flattened into UV space, like flattening a hide to make leather.
Complex models had their shells arranged across several UDIM tiles, so each texture stays small and easy to read.
Texturing used a node-based procedural workflow, which suits complicated surfaces better than layers.
Textures came from four sources, each chosen for what it does best.
Methods included hand-painting, stencils, procedural noise, tiling and projection.
Textures were checked constantly in a 3D view to confirm they land as intended.
Textures were exported as 2D maps for the animation software.
Materials were built from the maps and applied to the animated models.

o-vfx.s: Post-production starts with Laila's costume. Her hijab counters the stereotype of the oppressed Muslim woman, and its many folds needed careful study.
The costume was broken down into flat pattern pieces before draping.
The pieces were sewn and draped on Laila layer by layer, from the inside out.
Material properties, pins and welds tell the cloth how to behave once the body moves.
The cloth was simulated with every animated shot of Laila, then exported as four separate garments.
A semi-realistic look avoids the uncanny valley. Hair adds realism, but needs research to get right.
Laila's hair is mostly under her hijab, so only brows and lashes were groomed, on isolated scalps.
Little hair simulation was needed: the scalps simply follow the head.
Effects serve the story, not show off. The workstation's destruction, the major setback, was simulated as shattering rigid bodies.
Instead of a cliché fireball, a soft smoke drifts away in the aftermath, lit so the simulation could be judged.
Big and medium pieces come from rigid bodies; the finest debris comes from particles, following variation of shape.
Motion graphics show the characters' interactions with the lab's interfaces, revealing story information.

o-light.s: Light makes the shapes read in order of importance. A colour script planned the film's emotions in colour, as a guide rather than a rule.
Light was set on two levels: global lights for the single location, and lights tuned for each shot's moment.

items: Environment HDR, exterior and interior lights
Tuned per shot and per emotional moment

o-light.s: Quick test renders tuned each light's placement, intensity and colour before the final render.

o-render.s: For the final render, every shot was split three ways so each part could be adjusted later.

items: Key, fill, rim, bounce, kick, reflected
AOVs that add up to the beauty

o-render.s: Render passes (AOVs) are the components that add up to the final image, each adjustable on its own.
Objects were grouped into render layers, so important elements get their own control.
The render setup editor applied per-layer overrides through collections and sub-collections.
One machine was too slow, so a small render farm was built for the project.
With shots rendering out of order on several machines, a tracksheet tracked each shot's progress, reviewed every day.

o-comp.s: Compositing began by gathering every layer. Cloth-collision errors on Laila were painted out by hand with rotoscoping.
Each shot was rebuilt from its AOVs and light groups, then graded as a whole.
Green hills were painted from photos of Karimannoor and Munnar and projected onto simple geometry, instead of being modelled and rendered.
Shadows on projected backgrounds came from a single rendered shadow layer.
Glass was faked by blurring and grading the background, saving expensive transmission renders.
Motion blur was added in 2D from a motion-vector pass: not as accurate, but fast and noise-free.

o-comp.s: Rendered depth of field would have quadrupled render time, so it was rebuilt from a Z-depth pass using real camera values.

o-edit.s: The cut was largely set by the animatic and previz. The final edit joined the polished shots on one timeline and tuned the pacing.
